title: The same matter underlies the heavens
source_text: Ἔτι δὲ ἐπεί φησιν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον, σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις. καὶ ταύτῃ γε οὐδὲν διοίσει νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου ἢ ἀνθρώπου σῶμα· ὕλη γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ, καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτῶν ὅμοιον, λεκτέον καὶ πρὸς τοῦτον αὐτοῦ τὸν λόγον ὅτι εἴπερ. ἐπεὶ ἡ ὕλη ἡ αὐτὴ ὑπόκειται νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου ἢ ἀνθρώπου σώματι. οὐδὲν διοίσει ἀλλήλων ταῦτα τὰ σώματα. δηλονότι οὐδὲν διοίσει τὰ τούτων σώματα ἡλίου ἢ σελήνης ἢ ἀστέρων ἢ οὐρανοῦ ἢ οὑτινοσοῦν ἄλλου λεγομένου παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν αἰσθητοῦ θεοῦ. ὕλη γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ πᾶσι τοῖς σώμασιν ὑποκειμένη τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ ἄποιος καὶ ἀσχημάτιστος, τὰς ποιότητας οὐκ οἶδα κατὰ Κέλσον, τὸν μὴ θέλοντα φθαρτόν τι ἔργον εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ, ὑπὸ τίνος λαμβάνουσα. τὸ γὰρ φθαρτὸν ἀνάγκη παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὑποκειμένης ὕλης γεγενημένου ὅμοιον εἶναι κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον τῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ. εἰ μὴ ἄρα ἐνταῦθα ὁ Κέλσος θλιβόμενος ἀποπηδήσεται μὲν ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος, τοῦ ἔκ τινος κρατῆρος τὴν ψυχὴν ποιοῦντος, προσφεύξεται δὲ Ἀριστοτέλει καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ Περιπάτου, ἄϋλον φάσκουσιν εἶναι τὸν αἰθέρα, καὶ πέμπτης παρὰ τὰ τέσσαρα στοιχεῖα αὐτὸν εἶναι φύσεως· πρὸς ὃν λόγον οὐκ ἀγεννῶς καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς ἔστησαν. καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου καταφρονούμενοι στησόμεθα, ἀπαιτούμενοι διηγήσασθαι καὶ κατασκευάσαι τὸ ἐν τῷ προφήτῃ λεγόμενον οὕτως· „οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς· καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται, καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτοὺς [ὡς ἱμάτιον], καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ.“ πλὴν ἀρκεῖ πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον καὶ ταῦτα ἀποφηνάμενον ὅτι ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον, σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις· οὗ τῷ λόγῳ ἠκολούθησε μηδὲν διαφέρειν νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου σῶμα τοῦ αἰθερίου σώματος.
pass_a_gloss: Further, since Celsus says that soul is God's work, but of body another nature, and in this respect (ταύτῃ) the body of bat or worm or frog or man will differ in nothing; for the matter is the same and their corruptible alike — one must say (λεκτέον) to this argument (λόγος) of his that if, since the same matter underlies (ὑπόκειμαι) the body of bat or worm or frog or man, these bodies will differ in nothing from one another, plainly (δηλονότι) the bodies of these will differ in nothing from sun or moon or stars or heaven or any other called among the Greeks a perceptible god (αἰσθητὸς θεός). For the same matter underlying all bodies, by its own definition (ἴδιος λόγος) without quality (ἄποιος) and shapeless (ἀσχημάτιστος), I do not know from whom, according to Celsus who does not want anything corruptible to be God's work, it receives (λαμβάνω) the qualities. For the corruptible of anything whatever having come to be from the same underlying matter must (ἀνάγκη) be alike, according to Celsus by his own argument. Unless here Celsus, being pressed (θλίβω), will leap away (ἀποπηδάω) from Plato, who makes the soul from some mixing bowl (κρατήρ), and will flee for refuge (προσφεύγω) to Aristotle and those from the Peripatos, saying the ether (αἰθήρ) is immaterial (ἄϋλος) and of a fifth nature (πέμπτη φύσις) beside the four elements (στοιχεῖον); against which argument both those from Plato and those from the Stoa stood (ἵστημι) not ignobly. And we also, despised (καταφρονέω) by Celsus, shall stand, being required (ἀπαιτέω) to narrate (διηγέομαι) and establish what is said in the prophet thus: 'The heavens will perish (ἀπόλλυμι), but you will remain (διαμένω); and all will grow old (παλαιόω) like a garment (ἱμάτιον), and like a cloak (περιβόλαιον) you will roll (ἑλίσσω) them [like a garment], and they will be changed (ἀλλάσσω). But you are the same.' However it suffices against Celsus, having declared that soul is God's work, but of body another nature, from whose argument it followed (ἀκολουθέω) that the body of bat or worm or frog differs in nothing from the ethereal body (αἰθέριον σῶμα).
pass_b_english: Further, Celsus says: “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature. And in this respect the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog or a man will differ in nothing; for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.” To this argument of his too we must reply: if, because the same matter underlies the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog or a man, these bodies will differ in nothing from one another, then clearly the bodies of these creatures will differ in nothing from the sun or the moon or the stars or heaven, or from any other of those that the Greeks call gods perceived by the senses. For the same matter underlies all bodies, and by its own definition it is without quality and without shape. From whom it receives its qualities, on Celsus’s view, since he will not have anything perishable be a work of God, I do not know. For by Celsus’s own argument what is perishable in anything whatever that has come into being from the same underlying matter must be alike.

Unless, perhaps, hard pressed at this point, Celsus will leap away from Plato, who makes the soul out of a kind of mixing bowl (Plato, Timaeus 41d), and take refuge with Aristotle and the Peripatetics, who say that the ether is immaterial and is of a fifth nature beside the four elements. Against this argument both the followers of Plato and those of the Stoa have taken a stand, and done so with credit. And we too, whom Celsus despises, shall take a stand against it, since we are called upon to explain and establish what is said in the prophet as follows: “The heavens will perish, but you will remain; and they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same” (Psalm 102:26–27). Still, even these points are enough against Celsus, who declared that “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature.” From his argument it followed that the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog differs in nothing from the ethereal body.

choices.choice: Celsus's formula (4.52) aligned with the 4.chunk9 rendering: 'the soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature', 'maggot' for εὐλή, 'what is perishable in them is alike'
φθαρτόν rendered 'perishable' throughout; 'by its own definition'
οὐκ ἀγεννῶς ἔστησαν: 'have taken a stand, and done so with credit'; ἀπαιτούμενοι 'called upon'

Psalm citation: LXX Psalm 101:27–28 = English Psalm 102:26–27. Origen writes οἱ οὐρανοί where the LXX has αὐτοί (the subject is the heavens of the preceding verse). The staged text has [ὡς ἱμάτιον] after ἑλίξεις αὐτούς; square brackets in Koetschau mark words the editor deletes. The words appear in Hebrews 1:12 and were probably brought in from there. They are left out of the English and noted here. Timaeus 41d: the Demiurge mixes the soul in a mixing bowl (κρατήρ). αἰσθητὸς θεός: the heavenly bodies as gods perceived by the senses (compare Timaeus 40d on the visible gods); rendered 'gods perceived by the senses'. The opening quotation repeats Celsus's words from 4.52 exactly and is put in quotation marks; the closing reference to the same saying is also quoted. The final clause states what follows from Celsus's argument and is not quoted.
